lead: An oscillator makes a sine wave from a DC supply alone. It takes a feedback amplifier, returns a fraction β of the output to the input, and arranges that the returned signal arrives exactly in phase and exactly as large as needed. The circuit then feeds itself forever at one frequency f₀. This is positive feedback; the rule fixing f₀ and the minimum gain is the Barkhausen criterion. Transmitters, clocks, function generators and the local oscillator in every radio receiver depend on it.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for β and loop gain, and 4.3 for loop phase.

sections.h3: Positive feedback makes an amplifier feed itself

blocks.text: Negative feedback returns a fraction of the output so that it opposes the input, dropping gain to A/(1 + Aβ). Positive feedback returns it so that it adds. Add enough and the amplifier supplies its own input: the circuit oscillates.
Draw the loop as a summing node, an amplifier of gain A, and a network β that samples the output and returns part of it.

blocks.where: A is the open-loop voltage gain; β is the feedback fraction, the part of v_o returned; Aβ is the loop gain, dimensionless; v_o is the output voltage and v_s the external input, both in volts.

blocks.text: Set v_s to zero and allow v_o to be finite. That needs 1 − Aβ = 0, that is Aβ = 1. The closed-loop gain is then infinite: the smallest disturbance grows into a full-size sine.

sections.h3: The Barkhausen criterion: magnitude one, phase zero

blocks.text: Aβ is a complex number with a magnitude and a phase angle. The signal travelling once around the loop must come back with the same size and the same phase it started with, or each trip changes it.

blocks.where: ω₀ = 2πf₀ is the oscillation angular frequency in rad/s; f₀ is the oscillation frequency in Hz; ∠ means phase shift in degrees; n counts whole turns around the phase circle. Many books write the phase condition as 0°, which means the same thing.

blocks.text: The phase condition chooses f₀: only at one frequency does the total loop phase reach a whole multiple of 360°, so only there does the signal reinforce itself. The magnitude condition then sets the minimum gain, A ≥ 1/β.

Watch the sign bookkeeping. A common-emitter stage already inverts, giving 180°; its β network must supply the other 180° at f₀. A non-inverting stage starts at 0°, so its network supplies 0° or 360°.

sections.h3: Start-up, amplitude limiting, and what Barkhausen does not promise

blocks.text: A circuit with |Aβ| exactly 1 has no reason to start: zero output also satisfies the condition. Real circuits use |Aβ| slightly above 1 at f₀. Thermal noise and the switch-on transient contain every frequency; the f₀ component grows on each trip around the loop, the others do not.
Growth cannot continue forever. Something must pull the loop gain back to exactly 1 at the final amplitude:

items: The transistor cuts off on peaks and saturates on troughs, so the waveform clips and average gain falls.
Rectified base current charges the coupling capacitor and shifts the bias point, lowering gain as amplitude rises.
Diode limiters across the tank or the feedback path clip the return signal.
A thermistor or a small lamp in the β network changes β with amplitude, as in the Wien bridge.

blocks.text: Barkhausen is necessary but not sufficient for a clean sine. It says where and whether the circuit can oscillate; purity depends on how gently the limiting acts. Hard clipping gives a large third harmonic, a slow amplitude-dependent β a few percent distortion.
Oscillators are named after the network that sets f₀. The choice trades tuning range against frequency stability.

blocks.text: RC circuits are cheap and tune easily with a ganged capacitor or a potentiometer, which is why they dominate audio. LC circuits use a tapped tank to return just enough output. Crystal circuits use a quartz resonator whose very high Q holds f₀ almost fixed.

figure.caption: Noise at the summing node is amplified, and the β network returns it in phase. When the loop gain is one at f₀, the sine sustains itself with no external input.

spec.title: Oscillator loop
spec.aria: A vertical loop of noise into a summing node, then amplifier A, then output v_o, with the β network feeding back in phase so the loop gain is one at the oscillation frequency.

examples.question: A feedback amplifier has an inverting gain A = −50. Its feedback network has β = 0.02 and adds a further 180° of phase shift at 5 kHz. (a) Test the Barkhausen criterion and state the oscillation frequency. (b) The network is changed so that β = 0.03 at the same frequency. What happens to the amplitude and to the loop gain?
steps: Magnitude: |Aβ| = 1.0, so the magnitude condition is met exactly.
Phase: 180° from the inverting amplifier plus 180° from the network gives 360°, a whole multiple. The phase condition holds at 5 kHz.
Both conditions hold at 5 kHz, so the circuit oscillates at f₀ = 5 kHz.
For part (b), Aβ = (−50) × 0.03 = −1.5, so |Aβ| = 1.5, greater than 1.
Phase is unchanged, so f₀ stays 5 kHz but the amplitude grows on every trip: 1.5, 2.25, 3.375, and so on.
Growth stops when clipping or bias shift reduces the effective gain. The average |Aβ| then settles at 1, and the output is a steady but somewhat distorted sine.
examples.answer: The circuit satisfies Barkhausen at f₀ = 5 kHz with |Aβ| = 1 and total loop phase 360°; with β = 0.03 the loop gain magnitude becomes 1.5, so the amplitude grows until limiting brings the average loop gain back to 1.
examples.check:
A = -50
beta1 = 0.02
beta2 = 0.03
print(abs(A * beta1))
print(abs(180 + 180))
print(abs(A * beta2))

examples.question: A non-inverting amplifier (phase shift 0°) drives a feedback network that returns 5% of the output with no extra phase shift at 1.2 kHz. Find the loop gain if the amplifier gain is 15, and the minimum gain needed for oscillation.
steps: |Aβ| = 0.75 is less than 1, so the oscillation dies out even though the phase condition is met at 1.2 kHz.
With A = 20 the loop gain is exactly 1 and the circuit sustains oscillation at 1.2 kHz.
examples.answer: The loop gain is 0.75, below one, so it does not oscillate; the minimum amplifier gain for oscillation is 20.
examples.check:
beta = 0.05
A = 15
print(A * beta)
print(1 / beta)

traps: Checking only |Aβ| = 1 and forgetting the phase. Both conditions are needed; either alone proves nothing.
Leaving the amplifier's own 180° inversion out of the loop phase. A common-emitter stage plus a 180° network gives 360°, not 180°.
Using the negative-feedback denominator 1 + Aβ for a positive-feedback loop. Positive feedback gives 1 − Aβ, and the gain blows up as Aβ approaches 1.
Confusing this with the stability test of 4.3, where |Aβ| must fall below 1 by the time the phase reaches −180°. Here |Aβ| must reach 1 exactly at 0° or 360°.
Forgetting that the steady-state average |Aβ| equals 1, while the small-signal value is deliberately a little above 1 to start the oscillation.

quiz.q: State the Barkhausen criterion for oscillation.
quiz.a: At f₀ the loop gain must satisfy |Aβ| = 1 and the total loop phase must be a whole multiple of 360° (0°, 360°, 720°, …).

quiz.q: Why is a circuit built with |Aβ| exactly 1 at f₀ likely to stay silent?
quiz.a: Zero output also satisfies Aβ = 1, so the condition alone fixes no amplitude. A real circuit needs |Aβ| slightly above 1 so noise and the switch-on transient at f₀ grow each trip until limiting sets in.

quiz.q: An inverting amplifier has A = −40. Its β network returns 0.025 of the output and adds 180° at 2 kHz. Does it oscillate, and at what frequency?
quiz.a: Aβ = (−40)(0.025) = −1, so |Aβ| = 1. Total phase = 180° + 180° = 360°. Both conditions hold, so it oscillates at 2 kHz.

quiz.q: A non-inverting amplifier has β = 0.05 and the network contributes 0° at f₀. Find the minimum amplifier gain for oscillation.
quiz.a: A ≥ 1/β = 1/0.05 = 20. The phase condition is already met, so A must be at least 20.

quiz.q: An oscillator using a thermistor in its β network produces a cleaner sine than one relying on transistor clipping. Explain why.
quiz.a: The thermistor changes β smoothly with amplitude, so loop gain glides down to 1 without cutting the waveform. Clipping distorts the peaks, and a distorted wave carries harmonics. Gentle amplitude control keeps the transistor linear, so distortion stays small.

quiz.q: A student builds an RC phase shift oscillator and finds the output is zero although |Aβ| was measured as 1.01 at the design frequency. Give two likely reasons.
quiz.a: The small-signal loop gain may have been measured at a bias point the circuit never reaches, so it falls below 1 in practice; or the amplifier loading shifts the network phase so the phase condition is not exactly met. Check loop phase with the amplifier connected and raise gain so |Aβ| is comfortably above 1.

quiz.q: Which oscillator family would you choose for a 10 MHz radio local oscillator, and why?
quiz.a: A crystal oscillator, or an LC oscillator if the frequency must be tunable. A crystal gives stability of a few parts per million, which a 10 MHz radio stage needs; an RC network is far too unstable at that frequency.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real oscillators are judged by phase noise, the short-term random wander of f₀, which sets how clean a receiver or radar front end can be. Leeson's model relates phase noise to resonator Q and amplifier noise figure, explaining why quartz and ceramic resonators beat LC tanks. Silicon MEMS resonators now replace quartz in some consumer clocks because they seal in the same package as the chip. Frequency synthesis uses a phase-locked loop (Unit 7) to lock a tunable oscillator to a crystal reference.
